title: The Oil Merchant and the Silk Seller (PT)
summary: Two merchants dispute ownership of a purse of silver coins. Birbal drops the coins into boiling water to uncover the true owner. [PT]
full_text:
In the marketplace of Agra, a violent brawl erupted between an oil merchant named Teli Hira and a fine silk cloth merchant named Seth Mohan. Both men were clutching a leather purse containing fifty silver coins, each shouting: 'It is my purse! He stole it from my counter!'

The city watch brought both men before Emperor Akbar.

The oil merchant swore: 'Sire, I earned this silver selling mustard oil this morning! I dropped the purse by my barrel, and the silk seller snatched it!'

The silk merchant swore with equal fervor: 'Lies, Your Majesty! I received this silver from an Armenian merchant who bought three bolts of Benares silk from my shop! The purse is mine!'

There were no witnesses to the theft, and both men had high reputations in the bazaar. Akbar looked to Birbal for counsel.

Birbal examined the leather purse and the silver coins inside. He asked for a clean bronze bowl filled with boiling water from the palace kitchen.

Birbal tipped the purse, dropping the fifty silver coins into the steaming water.

The court leaned forward in curiosity.

Within seconds, a thin, glittering film of yellow oil floated to the surface of the hot water, and a distinct, sharp aroma of mustard oil filled the air!

Birbal smiled, pointing to the bowl:

'Behold, Your Majesty! Money handled by an oil merchant whose hands are constantly soaked in mustard oil absorbs grease into the pores of the silver coins.

'When dropped into boiling water, the oil floats to the top, carrying the scent of his shop. Had these coins belonged to a silk merchant, the water would remain clear, for silk merchants handle only dry, clean fabric!'

The silk merchant turned pale as chalk, fell to his knees, and confessed that he had stolen the purse while the oil merchant was filling a canister.

Akbar ordered the silver returned to the oil merchant, sentenced the silk merchant to thirty days in prison, and praised Birbal's brilliant application of natural science to justice.
